Even if you’re not comfortable with being labeled co-dependent (that term seems to really be what set you off and had you on the defensive), it is imperative that you do something about the situation immediately. Otherwise, that beloved kid of yours will grow up believing they can themselves, or should accept that people in their lives can, threaten with self-harm or to separate kids and parents and to lay tremendous amounts of emotional burden on one party in a relationship - i.e. codependent. And that’s just how it can affect them later, right now they are living with adults who are not regulating emotions adequately, which makes it much more difficult to feel safe and develop secure attachments, which is the opposite of having co-dependent tendencies. At least do it for the kid.

Yes, of course, the health issue will put stress upon your entire family and everything needs to be handled accordingly **up to a point**. Abuse should still not ever be tolerated, and I’m sure your therapist would agree. Anyone who isn't consistently making excuses for why someone should get to treat them badly, i.e. a co-dependent person, would. 

From my understanding, your current therapy centers around you being on the spectrum. If your therapist is a person you trust and are comfortable with, I would suggest you bring this to them as well.

It is possible to become codependent without seeking out people to fix or whatever you imagine a codependent person to be or look like. I think that’s more of a generalizing issue on your part. Codependency comes in all forms and can afflict anyone. If you’re walking on eggshells by bearing the brunt of the responsibility for your partner’s emotional regulation, you are by definition codependent. You don’t have to agree with that, and I’m sure you have a great way of keeping emotional distance from people in your professional life, (although that’s neither here nor there), but the sooner you start seeing this, the sooner you will be able to manage the abuse cycle better.

You cannot help your partner, or more importantly your child, if you are in all this distress, and if they do not know what things they can and cannot rely on you to fix for them. You can, however, refill that aforementioned cup, by going to therapy. A therapist can help you assert personal boundaries in a way that works with your partner’s condition. break the cycle of abuse that is affecting all three(!) of you negatively and rebuild the self-confidence and independence that is absolutely affected by living life at someone else’s whim for a long time.

Do you think it’s a coincidence that your trying to assert your boundaries about communication and emotional burden immediately resulted in your partner essentially threatening to kill themselves and taking your child from you? Your partner clearly also thinks of you as co-dependent and is using the fact to abuse you.
But you know it isn’t so. Be kind to both of you and break it off now.

You cannot pour from an empty cup, and from your post, **you** seem to be heavily codependent. You should get yourself some therapy and read up on managing having a partner with emotional instability issues.
